evidence: createApp sets up express, express.json() and route handlers: these are HTTP transport duties that belong in infrastructure.
Route handlers only read request.body, request.params and request.query, then hand off to service.createUser/createProject/createTask/listProjectTasks/assignTask/markTaskDone.
Error middleware turns DomainError into response.status(error.statusCode) and anything else into 500: this is transport-level error mapping.
No domain rules (such as status transitions or assignment checks) and no persistence logic in the file.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/http-server.ts passes. It is a transport adapter, and every responsibility in it belongs to the infrastructure layer. It sets up Express and registers routes, pulls raw values out of request bodies, params and queries, calls application-service methods, and turns results and errors into HTTP status codes and JSON. It has no business rules. It does not check task status, does not decide assignment eligibility, and does not validate domain invariants; those decisions are left to TaskManagementService. Two things looked borderline but are fine. First, the error handler turns DomainError into an HTTP response using error.statusCode. That code lives on the domain class, so if it is a problem, it belongs to a domain file outside this unit. The handler itself is ordinary transport error mapping. Second, the default `new TaskManagementService()` argument is light composition wiring, which suits the infrastructure layer. Import direction is out of scope for this check.
